title: Mumbai Air Worse Than Delhi's Again as Dust, Traffic and Still Winds Build Smog
excerpt: Mumbai topped India's pollution ranking on October 15 with an AQI of 152 and ranked third globally on October 20 at 166, as the Bombay High Court called the situation an emergency and demanded enforcement updates.
body:
• Mumbai recorded an AQI of 152 on October 15 — India's most polluted city that day and fifth globally on IQAir's list — the second time in 2026 its air has been worse than Delhi's, according to reporting cited by The CSR Journal.
  • Another IQAir-based ranking put Mumbai third globally on October 20 with an AQI of 166, ahead of Delhi at that time; in January and February this year Mumbai's AQI had reached around 400.
  • Experts blame construction dust, vehicle emissions, sluggish winds that trap pollutants, waste and garbage burning, agricultural fires and festival firecrackers — not a single seasonal cause.
  • For readers with family in Mumbai: check the daily AQI before outdoor exercise, keep children, older relatives and anyone with asthma or COPD indoors on poor days, and use a well-fitted N95 outdoors when exposure is unavoidable — pulmonologist Dr Sanggita Checker's advice, reported October 22.

The sea breeze is not saving Mumbai this time

Mumbai's air has deteriorated to levels worse than Delhi's — a comparison the city once assumed its sea breeze made impossible. On October 15, Mumbai recorded an Air Quality Index of 152, making it India's most polluted city that day and the fifth most polluted globally on IQAir's list, according to The CSR Journal. It was the second time in 2026 that Mumbai's air was worse than Delhi's, and it followed AQI readings around 400 in January and February.

https://x.com/ndtv/status/2114282720339841377

Days later the pattern repeated. An IQAir-based ranking reported Mumbai as the world's third most polluted city on October 20 with an AQI of 166, ahead of Delhi at that time, in coverage summarised by Trade Insight News. Air quality fluctuates through the day, so single readings are snapshots — but repeated snapshots in the same direction describe a trend, not an anomaly.

Why the pollutants are piling up

The familiar causes are construction dust and vehicle emissions, in a city carrying metro, coastal road and large redevelopment work at once. What has changed is the weather's ability to clear them. Atmospheric scientists cited in the reporting say wind speeds have fallen, allowing pollutants to accumulate close to the ground instead of being dispersed by the sea breeze. Unusually hot, humid weather after a rain-deficient monsoon has compounded the stagnation, and a Super El Niño influence on weather patterns was also cited.

Beyond traffic and construction, experts pointed to garbage burning in and around the city — including in areas south of Mumbai such as Alibaug, where waste is burned in the open for lack of proper disposal — agricultural fires further inland, and festival-season firecrackers despite regulations. Sensor readings near roadside garbage fires have shown high PM2.5 levels, the fine particles that penetrate deep into the lungs and worsen asthma, COPD and cardiovascular conditions.

The court calls it an emergency

The Bombay High Court has taken up the deterioration directly, describing the situation as an emergency and questioning how Mumbai could be more polluted than Delhi. The court sought updates from the police, the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation and the Maharashtra Pollution Control Board on enforcement action, and in related hearings criticised slow enforcement, poor public warning and violations involving firecrackers on streets, footpaths and near hospitals and schools. It warned that officers responsible for implementation could be held accountable for dereliction of duty.

That judicial pressure matters because Mumbai's sources are diffuse. Delhi's winter smog has a dominant seasonal driver; Mumbai's list — construction, traffic, waste burning, distant farm fires, firecrackers and weak winds — requires several agencies to act at once, which is exactly the coordination the court is demanding be reported back.

What residents should do on poor-AQI days

Dr Sanggita Checker, consultant pulmonologist at Wockhardt Hospitals, Mira Road, warned that people should not wait for visible smog before taking precautions. Senior citizens, pregnant women and children need extra protection because polluted air can aggravate respiratory conditions; persistent coughing, wheezing or breathlessness should prompt timely medical advice, and severe breathlessness or chest pain needs urgent care.

"Air pollution is no longer just an environmental concern; it is a serious public health challenge for Mumbai and nearby cities."

— Dr Sanggita Checker, Consultant Pulmonologist, Wockhardt Hospitals, Mira Road

The practical steps from that advice are concrete: check the daily AQI through official Central Pollution Control Board resources before planning outdoor exercise, keep children away from outdoor sports on poor days, avoid congested traffic corridors where possible, keep homes free of tobacco smoke, ventilate when outdoor air is cleaner, and use a properly fitted N95 mask when outdoor exposure is unavoidable. For diaspora readers, those are the specifics worth passing to parents and older relatives in Mumbai this week — along with the court's October 26 enforcement-update deadline, which will show whether the city's agencies have a plan beyond acknowledging the emergency.

items: Construction dust and vehicle emissions are major contributors.
Stagnant winds trap pollutants close to the ground.
Garbage burning and agricultural fires exacerbate the issue.
